editorial.summary: The episode opens with Asa Akira describing a spouse's reaction to a Yakuza Boy Instagram post. Because several people reportedly hold the account password, post authorship cannot be assigned from the handle alone. An explanation is explicitly withheld and remains withheld. David Choe compresses the Val/Yoshi janitorial and cast succession before the group begins Scruples. The commercial cards quickly give way to improvised yes/no moral scenarios. These range from warning a friend about infidelity or layoffs to drugging a rude customer, pregnancy deception, refusing emergency aid to an enemy, killing a friend, time travel, a venomous-spider bite, an impossible AIDS cure, survival choices and an incest-based alien cure. They are game hypotheticals, not admissions, intentions, medical claims or stable moral positions. Players revise premises, contradict answers, challenge one another and sometimes abandon questions. The archive preserves that instability. Before the game settles in, Episode 137's visible sexual encounter is retold. Steve says it happened out of nowhere; David argues he omitted extensive setup, including the partner's reported fantasies and a possible threesome discussion. Steve's shower refusal is repeated. Limited invitation, refusal, covert observation, later disclosure and visible sex remain separate. David says the Ranch recorded for two days and that the tape can settle what happened; another participant immediately demands deletion. Because the ambient recording is neither available nor authorized, it cannot become a truth oracle. A separate allegation says Bobby grabbed genitals during wrestling and previously forced hand-to-clothed-penis contact. The accounts remain attributed, not independently verified. Scruples reveals more about narrative behavior than answers: Steve is accused of omitting facts that make him look bad and adopting a nothing-is-my-fault pose; he says he felt warped and trapped by David and the partner. David's wealth is said to reduce hatred, while Steve's wrestling regret anchors the time-machine round. The brown-recluse and AIDS segments contain false or unreliable medical premises and are explicitly treated as fantasy. Near the end, a proposed scenario about someone within the group having sex and disclosure destroying the podcast is abandoned before an answer. It is not a new confession. The final exchange returns to the actual concern: are they now a prank-based group? Multiple people say they hate pranks. The audio stops mid-question with no formal sign-off.
